chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurara, that Durays had under him (as a wife) the daughter of Humran,

so he stipulated for her that he would not marry another wife upon her, and that he would not keep a concubine ever during her lifetime, nor after her death; upon a stipulation that she made for him that she would not marry after him; and they both stipulated upon themselves, from the sacrifice (hady), and the Hajj, and the sacrificial animal (badanah), and all their wealth to be for the poor, if one of them did not fulfill his obligation to the other.

Then he went to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and mentioned that to him. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'For the daughter of Humran there are rights, and that will not burden us so that we do not tell you the truth. Go and marry, and keep a concubine, for that (stipulation of hers) is not with anything (valid), and nothing is upon you nor upon her, and that which the two of you did is not with anything.' So he came, kept a concubine, and children were born to him after that.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on mutual stipulations in marriage contracts regarding remarriage and concubinage in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia juristic principle that marital stipulations (shurut) are valid as long as they do not contradict the essential nature of marriage (mu'at), a view championed by Imam al-Sadiq (AS). The ruling clarifies that while the husband promised not to take a concubine (surra), this was a binding contractual obligation rather than an invalidation of his inherent right, allowing him to fulfill the promise while retaining the legal capacity. This distinction underscores the flexibility of Shia family law in accommodating mutual agreements without altering the fundamental structure of the marital bond.
